case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in federal admiralty, a maritime contract’s choice-of-law clause is unenforceable when applying the chosen law would violate the strong public policy of the state whose law would otherwise govern.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2 (admiralty and maritime jurisdiction) and federal admiralty common law governing enforceability of contractual choice-of-law provisions in maritime contracts (in the background: Wilburn Boat’s approach to state law in marine insurance).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Great Lakes argues that federal maritime law should presumptively enforce choice-of-law clauses in marine insurance and other maritime contracts to promote uniformity, predictability, and international/commercial stability in maritime commerce. In its view, a state’s contrary public policy should not be able to override the parties’ contractual choice because admiralty is a federal domain and allowing 50-state policy overrides invites forum shopping and inconsistent outcomes; at most, enforcement should be refused only under narrow, federal maritime-law limits (e.g., traditional contract defenses) rather than a free-ranging ‘strong public policy of the displaced state’ test.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Raiders Retreat argues that even in admiralty, a choice-of-law clause should not be enforced when it would negate protections that reflect a strong public policy of the state with the most significant interest (here, the state whose law would apply absent the clause). It relies on the idea—drawn from The Bremen/Carnival’s ‘reasonableness’ framework—that maritime courts may refuse enforcement where doing so would contravene strong public policy, and it contends Wilburn Boat supports looking to state insurance law/policy in marine insurance disputes rather than rigidly enforcing contractual selections that evade state regulatory choices.
key_precedents: Wilburn Boat Co. v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 348 U.S. 310 (1955)
M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., 407 U.S. 1 (1972)
Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute, 499 U.S. 585 (1991)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language has a public-policy dimension and Wilburn Boat preserves substantial state regulatory interests in insurance. But that argument, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, conflates Wilburn Boat’s gap-filling about substantive rules with the antecedent, distinctly federal maritime question of whether a maritime choice-of-law clause is enforceable; importing a displaced State’s “fundamental policy” as a veto would predictably reintroduce disuniformity and forum shopping in the very domain admiralty is meant to regularize. Bremen’s public-policy carveout is better read here as a narrow, federally defined safety valve (traditional contract defenses and conflict with clearly established federal maritime policy), not a mechanism to constitutionalize fifty different state insurance regimes into the enforceability inquiry. A narrow opinion enforcing the clause on those federal terms addresses overreaching concerns without letting state policy swallow the federal admiralty presumption of enforcement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language can encompass refusal to enforce clauses that defeat a materially interested State’s fundamental insurance policy—does not overcome admiralty’s constitutional commitment to nationally uniform rules for maritime commerce. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wilburn Boat is a gap-filling decision about which substantive rule applies when federal maritime law is silent; it does not convert variable state regulatory preferences into a freestanding veto over the antecedent federal maritime question whether a choice-of-law clause is valid. On a textual and original public-meaning understanding of Article III’s admiralty grant, Bremen’s public-policy safety valve is best read as a narrow, federally defined limitation (traditional contract defenses or conflict with clearly established federal maritime policy), not a mechanism to incorporate fifty different state “fundamental policies” and invite forum shopping and disuniformity. Nothing in Justice Jackson’s proposed “cabined” exception supplies a historically grounded, administrable federal standard for selecting which state policy controls without dissolving the uniform federal rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-based synthesis—reading Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language to incorporate a materially interested State’s fundamental insurance policies in standardized contracts—has intuitive appeal, but it effectively converts a narrow federal admiralty safety valve into a fifty-state public-policy override that defeats the uniformity rationale Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes. Wilburn Boat, as Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, is properly understood as gap-filling on substantive insurance rules when no federal maritime rule exists; it does not authorize state policy to negate the antecedent federal maritime rule that presumptively enforces choice-of-law clauses. Under my textualist, consequence-attentive approach, letting state “nonwaivable” protections control enforceability invites forum shopping and unpredictability in maritime commerce, while Bremen’s exception is better confined to traditional contract defenses and conflicts with clearly established federal maritime policy. That leaves room to police true overreaching without turning state regulatory preferences into a general veto over maritime contracting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s uniformity concern is the strongest point for Petitioner, but it overreads Bremen as if its “unreasonable or unjust” safety valve were limited to a purely federal-maritime public policy; Bremen itself contemplates nonenforcement when a clause would defeat a materially interested jurisdiction’s fundamental policy, and marine insurance is a domain where Wilburn Boat recognizes especially weighty state regulatory interests. Justice Kagan’s proposed “federally defined only” exception is more administrable, but it risks making the federal presumption an instrument for sophisticated insurers to draft around nonwaivable state insured-protective rules in standardized contracts—an outcome that, in real-world effect, undermines access to meaningful insurance protections for less powerful parties. The way to respect both uniformity and fairness is a strong presumption of enforcement coupled with a genuinely narrow, fact-bound Bremen reasonableness inquiry that asks whether the chosen law would strip core, nonwaivable protections of the otherwise-applicable state with the greater interest and whether the insured had meaningful bargaining power. That keeps most maritime contracting predictable while preventing uniformity from becoming a one-way ratchet that facilitates overreaching in regulated insurance relationships.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language has sometimes encompassed a public-policy inquiry, and Wilburn Boat recognizes significant state interests in regulating marine insurance. But as Chief Justice Roberts notes, that argument skips the antecedent question—whether the enforceability of a maritime choice-of-law clause is itself governed by a federal maritime rule aimed at uniformity; if it is, importing each displaced State’s “fundamental policy” as an independent veto would predictably recreate the very disuniformity and forum shopping admiralty jurisdiction is designed to prevent. On my pragmatic textualist view, the administrable synthesis is a federally defined reasonableness exception (traditional contract defenses and conflict with clearly established federal maritime policy), rather than a free-ranging state-policy override that would swallow the presumption of enforcement. Wilburn Boat remains relevant to gap-filling on substantive insurance rules once applicable law is determined, but it does not authorize private-party drafting disputes to turn federal enforceability into a 50-state policy referendum.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly press that The Bremen speaks of “unreasonable or unjust” enforcement and mentions “strong public policy,” particularly salient in insurance. But read in its admiralty context, that language supplies a federally administered safety valve (fraud, overreaching, practical denial of a day in court, or conflict with a clearly established federal maritime policy), not an invitation to treat each State’s regulatory preferences as a trump over the federal maritime rule favoring enforcement—an approach that would defeat the Constitution’s admiralty-related interest in uniformity and predictability, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. Wilburn Boat, as Justice Kagan notes, is a gap-filler for substantive insurance rules where no federal maritime rule exists; it does not authorize state policy to negate the antecedent federal question whether the parties’ maritime choice-of-law clause is valid and enforceable. Absent a traditional contract defense or a specific, established federal maritime policy against enforcement, I would enforce the clause and leave any further substantive-rule selection to the law the parties chose.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language can include a public-policy limitation, and that Wilburn Boat preserves meaningful state regulatory interests in marine insurance. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that argument collapses the antecedent question—whether a maritime choice-of-law clause is enforceable under federal maritime law—into a fifty-state “fundamental policy” veto that would predictably reintroduce disuniformity and forum shopping, undermining admiralty’s constitutional commitment to uniform rules. I read Bremen’s public-policy carveout, in this maritime-contract setting, as a narrow, federally defined safety valve (alongside traditional contract defenses), not an invitation to incorporate the displaced State’s insurance policies wholesale; Wilburn Boat is gap-filling on substantive insurance rules where no federal rule exists, not permission for state policy to override the established federal presumption enforcing such clauses. Nothing presented in conference shows a clearly established federal maritime policy against enforcing this kind of clause, so I would enforce it absent fraud, coercion, or similar defects.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counter: The Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” language includes a public-policy limit, and Wilburn Boat preserves substantial state authority over marine-insurance regulation, so a choice-of-law clause should not become a device to evade nonwaivable state protections. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that argument conflates two distinct questions: Wilburn Boat is gap-filling on substantive marine-insurance rules when no established federal maritime rule exists, whereas the threshold enforceability of a maritime choice-of-law clause is itself governed by an established federal maritime presumption favoring enforcement to secure uniformity. Textually and structurally, Article III’s admiralty grant supports a uniform federal rule on validity; reading Bremen’s public-policy carveout to incorporate whichever displaced State claims a “fundamental policy” would convert a narrow federal exception into a fifty-state veto and reintroduce the forum shopping admiralty jurisdiction was meant to reduce. I would therefore enforce the clause absent traditional contract defenses (fraud, coercion, unconscionability) or conflict with a clearly established federal maritime policy, not a free-ranging incorporation of state insurance policy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively stress that the enforceability standard for a maritime choice-of-law clause is a federal maritime question, and that a broad state-policy veto could erode uniformity and invite forum shopping. But their reading narrows The Bremen’s “unreasonable or unjust” inquiry too far: Bremen itself contemplates nonenforcement where enforcement would contravene a strong public policy of a jurisdiction with a materially greater interest, and Wilburn Boat underscores that state insurance regulation is not a mere “preference” but a structural allocation of authority when federal maritime law has not supplied the substantive rule. A pragmatic, administrable middle path is to treat the public-policy exception as genuinely cabined—limited to clearly articulated, fundamental, nonwaivable insured-protective rules of the otherwise-applicable State in standardized coverage settings—rather than a free-ranging balancing test. On that view, enforcing the clause here to displace core state insurance safeguards risks practical unfairness and undermines Wilburn Boat’s accommodation without delivering the kind of predictable uniformity Roberts envisions, because the predictable consequence would be private end-runs around nonwaivable state protections.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III’s grant of admiralty jurisdiction reflects a strong federal interest in uniform rules for maritime commerce, and our cases generally presume enforcement of contractual forum and law selections in maritime agreements absent narrow, well-defined exceptions. Under M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. and Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute, the federal maritime-law inquiry is whether enforcement is unreasonable, unjust, or otherwise invalid under traditional contract defenses—not whether the displaced State has a “strong public policy” that would be undermined. Wilburn Boat permits state law to fill gaps only where no established federal maritime rule exists; the enforceability of choice-of-law clauses in maritime contracts is an area where federal admiralty has long supplied a presumption of enforceability to promote predictability and uniformity. A narrow holding enforcing the clause subject to Bremen-style limits best preserves maritime uniformity and institutional legitimacy while leaving States room to regulate through generally applicable doctrines and federal statutory constraints where Congress has spoken.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2 vests admiralty and maritime jurisdiction in the federal courts, and the historical premise of admiralty is national uniformity rather than state-by-state variation. Under The Bremen and Carnival Cruise, maritime courts presumptively enforce contractual clauses absent narrow, contract-like defects (fraud, overreaching, or truly unreasonable terms), and a free-ranging “strong public policy of the displaced state” veto is not a traditional limitation in federal maritime law. Wilburn Boat allows resort to state law only when there is no established federal maritime rule; here, the federal maritime rule favoring enforcement of bargained-for choice-of-law clauses supplies the rule of decision and should not yield to divergent state insurance policies. Allowing state public policy to override these clauses would invite forum shopping and erode the uniform maritime law the Constitution presupposes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: In admiralty under Article III, § 2, enforceability of a maritime contract’s choice-of-law clause is a question of federal maritime common law, and allowing a displaced state’s “strong public policy” to invalidate such clauses would undermine uniformity and invite forum shopping. Wilburn Boat recognizes that state law may fill gaps in marine insurance only where no established federal maritime rule applies, but it does not authorize states to override federal admiralty rules governing the validity of contractual choice-of-law provisions. The Bremen’s “unreasonable” exception—developed for forum-selection clauses—does not justify a free-ranging incorporation of fifty different state policies into federal admiralty choice-of-law enforcement, and Carnival Cruise underscores the practical commercial need for predictable, enforceable contractual provisions in maritime commerce. The better rule is a strong presumption of enforcement subject only to narrow, federally defined limits (e.g., traditional contract defenses or conflict with a federal maritime policy), not a generalized state-public-policy veto.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Federal admiralty recognizes a presumption that contractual choice-of-law clauses are enforceable, but that presumption has long been subject to a “reasonableness” limitation, including refusal where enforcement would contravene a strong public policy of a jurisdiction with a materially greater interest in the dispute. Under M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. and Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute, maritime courts need not enforce contractual provisions that operate unfairly or unjustly in practice—especially where they would strip state-law protections designed for insureds and other vulnerable parties. Wilburn Boat confirms that, absent an established federal maritime rule on the substantive insurance issue, state law ordinarily supplies the rule of decision; it would be inconsistent with that framework to let a choice-of-law clause categorically evade the strong public policy of the state whose law would otherwise govern. Accordingly, the clause should be unenforceable to the extent it would defeat that state’s fundamental protective policy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: In admiralty, the starting point is a federal common-law preference for enforcing contractual choice-of-law provisions to promote predictability and uniformity in maritime commerce, and this Court’s reasoning in M/S Bremen v. Zapata and Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute supports enforcing bargained-for clauses absent narrow, well-defined exceptions. Wilburn Boat teaches that state law fills gaps only when there is no established federal maritime rule; but the enforceability of a choice-of-law clause in a maritime contract is itself a federal admiralty question that should not turn on a free-ranging “strong public policy” override pegged to whichever state’s law would otherwise apply. Allowing each state’s public policy to defeat the parties’ selection would invite forum shopping and undermine statutory and commercial coherence across the maritime domain contemplated by Article III’s admiralty jurisdiction. A limited federal public-policy exception—cabined to fundamental illegality or traditional contract defenses—best balances workability with respect for state interests without letting state policy swallow maritime uniformity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III’s grant of admiralty jurisdiction presupposes a body of federal maritime law that favors uniform rules for maritime commerce, and that traditional aim is undermined if each State’s “strong public policy” may override the parties’ chosen law in a maritime contract. Under M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. and Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute, maritime courts presumptively enforce forum/choice clauses absent narrow, recognized grounds (e.g., fraud, overreaching, or contravention of a controlling federal maritime policy), not a free-ranging inquiry into the displaced State’s policy preferences. Wilburn Boat does not compel a different result because it addresses gap-filling with state substantive law where no established federal maritime rule exists; the enforceability of contractual choice-of-law provisions is itself an established feature of federal maritime law aimed at predictability. Respecting the contract’s text and the federal interest in uniformity, I would enforce the clause unless it violates a federal maritime policy or other traditional contract defense applies.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: In admiralty under Article III, federal maritime law has long pursued uniform, workable rules for maritime commerce, and that objective strongly supports presumptive enforcement of maritime choice-of-law clauses absent narrow, traditional limits. M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. and Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute reflect a federal maritime-law framework favoring enforcement of freely negotiated contractual provisions, with only a limited public-policy exception grounded in federal maritime policy—not a free-ranging incorporation of each displaced state’s “strong public policy.” Allowing state public policy to negate the parties’ chosen law would reintroduce the very disuniformity and forum shopping federal admiralty is designed to avoid, and Wilburn Boat does not compel that result because it addresses gaps in federal maritime rules rather than authorizing states to override federal enforceability principles for contractual clauses. The better, restrained approach is to enforce the clause unless it is invalid under traditional contract defenses or contravenes a clearly established federal maritime policy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III’s grant of admiralty jurisdiction presupposes a federal maritime law that prizes uniform rules for maritime commerce, and a federal default of enforcing maritime contract terms—including choice-of-law clauses—best fits that historical understanding. The Bremen and Carnival Cruise establish a strong presumption that freely negotiated maritime clauses are enforceable, subject to narrow, federal limits; their “strong public policy” carveout is not a license to import the varying public policies of whichever State’s law would otherwise apply. Wilburn Boat does not compel the Third Circuit’s approach, because it addressed the absence of an established federal rule on specific marine-insurance issues and does not authorize state public policy to negate a generally applicable federal maritime rule favoring contractual choice-of-law. Allowing state-policy overrides would undermine predictability and invite forum shopping, contrary to the methodological consistency of federal admiralty common law.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III’s admiralty grant supports federal oversight, but Wilburn Boat teaches that absent an established federal maritime rule, state law fills the gap in marine insurance—particularly where states have strong regulatory interests. The Bremen and Carnival enforce maritime contractual clauses only so long as enforcement is not “unreasonable or unjust,” and that reasonableness inquiry has long included refusing enforcement that would contravene a strong public policy of the forum (or the state with the most significant interest). Allowing a choice-of-law clause to negate core state insurance protections would undermine procedural fairness and practical consequences for insureds, especially where the state’s policy is aimed at preventing overreaching in standardized coverage. Thus, the clause should be unenforceable to the extent it would displace the otherwise-applicable state law embodying a strong public policy.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under federal admiralty law, a choice-of-law clause in a maritime contract (here, a marine insurance policy) is unenforceable when applying the chosen law would violate the strong public policy of a different State whose law would otherwise apply.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2 (admiralty and maritime jurisdiction) and federal maritime common law governing enforceability of contractual choice-of-law clauses (as informed by cases such as The Bremen and Wilburn Boat).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Great Lakes argues that in admiralty the enforceability of a choice-of-law clause is a question of federal maritime law and should be enforced to promote uniformity and predictability in maritime commerce, and that a displaced State’s public policy should not be able to invalidate the clause; otherwise, marine insurance contracts become subject to forum-by-forum variation and strategic pleading that undermines national and international maritime contracting.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Raiders Retreat argues that even in admiralty, a choice-of-law clause cannot be enforced when it would defeat the strong public policy of the State with the most significant interest (here, the State whose law would apply absent the clause), and that Wilburn Boat’s approach to marine insurance permits application of state law and state insurance policy judgments—so a federal court should refuse enforcement where the chosen law would nullify state-protective insurance rules.
key_precedents: Wilburn Boat Co. v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 348 U.S. 310 (1955)
M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., 407 U.S. 1 (1972)
Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute, 499 U.S. 585 (1991)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Wilburn Boat point rightly underscores the States’ historic primacy in regulating insurance and cautions against gratuitous federal common lawmaking, but it does not resolve the antecedent question whether a maritime choice-of-law clause is enforceable as a matter of federal maritime law. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, The Bremen/Carnival Cruise supply a settled, administrable federal framework presuming enforcement of selection clauses absent fraud, overreaching, or contravention of a controlling federal maritime policy; converting that inquiry into a forum State’s freestanding “strong public policy” veto would erode maritime uniformity and invite forum shopping. A minimalist path is to hold only that federal maritime law governs enforceability and that state policy concerns go to the substantive rule only after a valid clause is enforced, consistent with Wilburn Boat’s gap-filling role. Nothing in Wilburn Boat compels empowering States to displace an existing federal maritime rule about contractual selection provisions, and doing so would unnecessarily destabilize predictable maritime contracting.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wilburn Boat does not overcome the antecedent point, emphasized by Justice Kagan and Justice Alito, that enforceability of a maritime choice-of-law clause is itself a federal admiralty question governed by a presumptive federal rule of enforcement. Wilburn Boat addresses the content of substantive marine-insurance doctrines when federal maritime law supplies no rule; it does not authorize a forum State to nullify the parties’ contractual law selection at the threshold based on a freestanding state “strong public policy.” Under the original public meaning of Article III’s admiralty grant, uniformity in maritime contracting is the baseline, and the “public policy” limitation described in The Bremen must be anchored in controlling federal maritime policy (or statute), not whichever State’s insurance regime a plaintiff can invoke by forum choice. I therefore remain with the Petitioner: the clause should be enforced absent fraud, overreaching, or conflict with a specifically identified federal maritime policy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-and-state-regulation point has intuitive appeal, but it still conflates Wilburn Boat’s gap-filling instruction about substantive marine-insurance doctrines with the antecedent question whether a maritime choice-of-law clause is enforceable under federal maritime law. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, The Bremen and Carnival Cruise supply a federal admiralty rule of presumptive enforcement, with any “public policy” limitation properly anchored in controlling federal maritime policy or federal statutory constraints—not a forum State’s variable insurance policy preferences. Accepting Sotomayor’s broader state-policy veto at the enforcement stage would, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, reintroduce the very unpredictability and forum shopping admiralty jurisdiction is meant to minimize, and it would do so without a textual or precedential basis for displacing the federal rule governing selection clauses. I therefore remain with the Petitioner and would frame the holding narrowly to preserve Wilburn Boat’s role downstream while keeping enforceability uniform upstream.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan fairly press the distinction between (1) the threshold enforceability of a maritime choice-of-law clause and (2) the substantive rule supplied by state law under Wilburn Boat, and they are right that uniformity and predictability are real admiralty values. But The Bremen and Carnival Cruise’s pro-enforcement presumption is not a blank check: their “unreasonable” and “fundamentally unfair” limits must be applied with attention to the practical effect here—allowing an insurer to contract around mandatory, policyholder-protective insurance rules that a State has adopted to level bargaining disparities and prevent surprise forfeitures. Wilburn Boat matters because it reflects a longstanding understanding that marine insurance is not an area of entrenched federal maritime doctrine and that state insurance regulation is primary; I do not read our forum/choice cases as silently creating a federal common-law rule that preempts a State’s core insurance public policy whenever parties insert a clause. So even accepting Justice Kagan’s workability concerns about forum shopping, I would not displace Pennsylvania’s protective regime absent a clearly established federal maritime policy requiring enforcement in these circumstances.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/public-policy point has intuitive pull in the insurance context, but it still depends on reading Wilburn Boat as authorizing a threshold state-law veto over enforceability, and Wilburn Boat is about substantive gap-filling once the governing law is identified, not the antecedent validity of the parties’ maritime choice-of-law agreement. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is persuasive on that sequencing: The Bremen/Carnival Cruise supply an administrable federal maritime rule presuming enforcement, with the “public policy” limitation best understood—as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize—as anchored to controlling federal maritime policy (or statute), not variable forum-state insurance policies. Pragmatically, importing a free-floating “strong state public policy” exception at the enforcement stage would predictably invite forum shopping and defeat admiralty’s uniformity function, while still leaving room for state insurance rules to operate in the substantive gap-filling space Wilburn Boat describes. I therefore see no legal argument that undermines the narrower, uniform federal enforceability rule we’ve discussed.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Wilburn Boat point is the best pushback, but it still targets the wrong stage: Wilburn Boat concerns what substantive rule governs marine-insurance disputes when federal maritime law is silent, not whether a maritime choice-of-law clause is enforceable in the first instance. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain, The Bremen/Carnival Cruise supply a federal maritime rule of presumptive enforceability, and the “public policy” exception must be tied to a controlling federal maritime policy (or statute), not a forum State’s insurance preferences that would vary case by case. Under an originalist understanding of Article III’s admiralty grant, allowing a non-chosen State to veto the clause would defeat maritime uniformity and invite forum shopping. Sotomayor’s fairness concern is real, but absent fraud/overreaching or a specifically federal prohibition, it cannot justify rewriting the parties’ maritime contract under a free-floating state public-policy test.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s concern about insurers contracting around mandatory state protections is serious, but it presupposes that a forum State’s “strong public policy” can defeat a maritime choice-of-law clause at the threshold—an approach that, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, would reintroduce the very forum-by-forum unpredictability admiralty is meant to prevent. Wilburn Boat, on my reading, is about what substantive rule applies when federal maritime law is silent, not an invitation for states to override an established federal maritime contract rule governing enforceability of selection clauses. Under The Bremen/Carnival Cruise, the “public policy” exception is best understood as anchored in a controlling federal maritime policy (or statute), not a movable target defined by whichever non-chosen State’s policy is invoked. Institutionally and as a matter of workability, a uniform federal enforceability rule with narrow exceptions (fraud/overreaching or conflict with federal maritime policy) remains the sounder course.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Wilburn Boat point remains the most serious counter: it cautions against manufacturing federal maritime rules in marine insurance and highlights States’ traditional regulatory interests. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that case concerns the substantive rule of decision when maritime law is silent—not the antecedent enforceability of a contractual choice-of-law clause, which our maritime-contract precedents (The Bremen and Carnival Cruise) treat as a federal maritime question with a presumption of enforcement. Textually and historically, Article III’s admiralty grant presupposes national uniformity for maritime contracting, and allowing a non-chosen forum State’s “strong public policy” to invalidate the clause would reintroduce the very forum-by-forum variability admiralty jurisdiction is meant to avoid. I therefore read the “public policy” limit in Bremen as referring to controlling federal maritime policy (or statute), not a free-standing state veto, leaving Wilburn Boat to operate only after a valid law-selection clause is honored.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s core fairness concern—that insurers could use choice-of-law clauses to evade mandatory state insurance protections—has real force, especially given Wilburn Boat’s respect for state regulation in marine insurance. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Wilburn Boat speaks to the substantive rule of decision when federal maritime law is silent; it does not authorize a threshold, forum-state “strong public policy” veto over enforceability of maritime selection clauses, which The Bremen/Carnival Cruise treat as governed by a federal, presumptively pro-enforcement standard. Under a progressive pragmatist lens, administrability and evenhandedness matter: letting any non-chosen State’s policy invalidate the clause would predictably incentivize forum shopping and produce unequal outcomes for similarly situated insureds depending on filing location. States can still protect policyholders through substantive gap-filling once the clause is enforced, but the enforceability rule itself should remain a uniform federal maritime one absent fraud, overreaching, or a specifically identified controlling federal maritime policy to the contrary.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Article III’s grant of admiralty jurisdiction, federal maritime law has a strong interest in uniform rules that promote predictability in maritime commerce, and this Court has generally enforced contractual selection provisions absent a compelling federal-law reason to refuse. Consistent with M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. and Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute, a maritime choice-of-law clause should be presumptively enforceable, with invalidation turning on federal maritime public policy rather than the forum State’s contrary policy. Wilburn Boat permits state law to fill gaps in marine insurance only where there is no established federal maritime rule; here, adopting a narrow federal rule governing enforceability of the choice-of-law clause preserves uniformity without broadly displacing state insurance regulation. Accordingly, a different State’s public policy should not, by itself, render the clause unenforceable in admiralty when the clause is otherwise valid under federal maritime law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2’s grant of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction presupposes a federal law of the sea sufficient to secure national uniformity in maritime commerce, and the enforceability of a contractual choice-of-law clause is properly treated as a question of federal maritime law. Under this Court’s maritime-contract cases, choice clauses are presumptively enforceable and may be disregarded only on limited federal grounds (e.g., fraud, overreaching, or contravention of a controlling federal maritime policy), not because a different State would prefer a contrary insurance rule. Wilburn Boat holds only that, absent an established federal maritime rule on the substantive insurance issue, state law may fill the gap; it does not authorize a forum State’s “strong public policy” to defeat the parties’ contractual selection of governing law as a matter of federal admiralty enforceability. Consistent with M/S Bremen and Carnival Cruise, enforcing the clause promotes predictability and uniformity and prevents state-by-state variation from undermining maritime contracting.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: In admiralty, the enforceability of contractual choice-of-law provisions is a question of federal maritime law, and federal law has long favored enforcing freely negotiated maritime contract clauses to promote uniformity and predictability in maritime commerce. Under M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., such clauses are presumptively valid and may be set aside only for a narrow, traditionally federal “strong public policy” exception—not a freewheeling incorporation of differing state insurance policies that would recreate the very forum-by-forum variation admiralty jurisdiction is meant to avoid. Wilburn Boat does not justify allowing state public policy to override a contractual choice-of-law clause as a threshold matter; at most it addresses when state substantive rules may fill gaps absent an established federal maritime rule. Allowing displacement by a State’s policy preferences would undermine practical consequences central to maritime contracting and is inconsistent with the pro-enforcement approach reflected in decisions like Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III’s admiralty grant does not require that every marine-insurance issue be governed by a uniform federal rule, and Wilburn Boat instructs that where there is no established federal maritime rule, state law supplies the rule of decision for marine insurance contracts. That principle leaves room for a State with the most significant interest—particularly one regulating insurance and protecting policyholders—to refuse enforcement of a choice-of-law clause that would contravene its strong public policy. The Bremen and Carnival Cruise enforced selection clauses to promote predictability, but they also recognize limits where enforcement would be unreasonable or fundamentally unfair, and allowing insurers to contract around core state insurance protections would have real-world consequences for vulnerable insureds. Absent a clearly established federal maritime rule compelling enforcement even against strong state policy, I would not displace Pennsylvania’s protective insurance judgments here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: In admiralty, the enforceability of contractual forum- and law-selection provisions is a question of federal maritime common law, and our cases make such clauses presumptively enforceable to promote uniformity and predictability in maritime commerce.
